newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain's Labour takes EU social policy step.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour takes EU social policy step.

text.p: The EU's Social Affairs Council will try on Friday to reach a common position on a directive to make it easier for employees to win sex discrimination suits in a debate that will include Britain's new Labour government.
The former Conservative government did not participate in talks over the legislation because of its "opt out" from some EU workplace regulations under the Maastricht Treaty's Social Protocol.

Prime Minister Tony Blair told his EU counterparts at last week's Amsterdam summit that Britain now wanted to sign up to the protocol, which will be incorporated into the new treaty agreed at the summit.
The Council in Luxembourg will give Britain its first chance to reverse course.

The proposal for a new EU sex-discrimination directive, COM(96)93, aims to ensure that employers share the burden of proof when they are sued. It says workers must first establish before a court or other competent authority "facts from which it can be presumed that there has been direct or indirect discrimination".
The employer would then have to prove that it had not violated the principle of equal treatment.

Britain cannot play a formal role in debates under the Social Protocol until the new treaty is ratified. However, the summit leaders agreed that other countries would take account of its views in adopting such legislation.
In this case, Britain wants the text to state that its own system of handling sex-discrimination suits through industrial tribunals meets the terms of the directive, diplomats said.

Under that system, once an employee has established prima facie evidence of discrimination, he or she wins the case if the employer fails to respond or provides an evasive or unsatisfactory response, they said.

One outstanding issue involves the directive's scope. The current text says it applies to EU treaty language on equal pay (Article 119), EU directives on equal pay (75/117/EEC) and access to jobs, training and promotions (76/207/EEC) and sex-discrimination aspects of EU laws on the health and safety of pregnant workers (92/85/EEC) and parental leave (96/34/EEC)

The European Commission wants it to cover additional EU directives on social security schemes (86/378/EEC) and equal treatment of self-employed men and women (86/613/EEC) while Italy wants it to apply to all EU measures involving equal treatment, diplomats said.
